title: Build a three-tier can pyramid on a shop display mat
instruction: Build a pyramid display of the six cans on the green mat: three in the bottom row, two on those, and one on top.
context: Stockers and order fillers (2.8 million US workers) stock shelves and build merchandise displays as regular work; can pyramids on promotion end caps are among the commonest. Each upper can rests across two cans below it, so the bottom row has to sit close enough for both supports, every can has to be set down upright and centred, and placing the upper tiers must not knock the ones already built.
setup: Fixed layout as in the screenshot (x forward from the robot base, y to its left, heights from the table top). A light grey vinyl counter cover (90 x 100 x 0.3 cm) covers the table. A green felt display mat (12 cm deep, 26 cm wide, 0.2 cm thick) is centred 32 cm out and 12 cm left. Six identical tinplate steel food cans (6.8 cm across, 6 cm tall, flat ends, red paper label, 300 g) stand upright on a plywood delivery tray (22 x 26 x 0.4 cm, centred 20 cm out, 37 cm left) in two rows of three: 14 cm and 26 cm out, at 29, 37 and 45 cm left. Behind the mat, a yellow card price sign (0.8 x 10 x 8 cm) stands on edge 43 cm out, 12 cm left. At the back, out of reach, is a shop shelf unit: a white painted plywood back panel (2 x 80 x 30 cm) 71 cm out, with two grey steel shelves (10 x 80 x 1.2 cm) 66 cm out at the counter and 12 cm up, each holding eight fixed stock cans of the same size (red labels below, green above), 8.5 cm apart.
scoring: 0 if any can ends tipped more than 45 degrees, or standing on a single can as in a tower (its centre within 1.5 cm of that can's centre and its base within 1 cm of that can's top). Otherwise, a can counts when it stands upright (within 10 degrees) and at rest. 0.25 for a bottom row: three cans with their bases on the mat (within 1 cm) and centres inside it, in a straight line (the middle centre within 1 cm of the line through the outer two) with neighbouring centres 6.6 to 8.3 cm apart and the outer two at least 12.6 cm apart. 0.5 if two more cans each bridge a different neighbouring pair of that row. 1.0 if a sixth can bridges those two. A can bridges two cans when their centres are 6.6 to 8.3 cm apart, its centre is within 1.5 cm of the midpoint between them, and its base is within 1 cm of both their tops. A can on any other object adds nothing. Anything else scores 0.
reset_notes: Return the six cans to the tray positions.
fidelity: Rigid bodies only. The cans are flat-ended steel cylinders at the size of a small food can; real cans have rolled rims, which make bridging slightly less stable. Every surface has the same rubber-like friction (1.2). The stock cans on the shelf are fixed scenery.
